titre: Hegel Does Not Describe His Philosophy as “Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis”
accroche: The triangle drawn to sum up Hegel takes up Fichte's vocabulary, which Hegel did not adopt for his own philosophy
contenu_vulgarise:
On the board, a teacher draws a triangle: thesis at the top, antithesis at bottom left, synthesis at bottom right. “That is Hegel's dialectic,” he says. The image has become common. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy speaks of a traditional idea, according to which Hegel's dialectic would follow this scheme, and notes that the first moments of his logic (Being, Nothing, Becoming) serve as the “textbook” example. But Hegel did not adopt this vocabulary to describe his own philosophy.

## What Hegel Actually Writes

In the Logic of the *Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences* (here in William Wallace's English translation), Hegel distinguishes, in paragraphs 79 to 82, three “sides” of the logical doctrine: the abstract side, that of the understanding; the dialectical side, that of negative reason; the speculative side, that of positive reason. He specifies that these sides do not form three parts of logic: they are stages, “moments,” present in every concept and every truth. In these paragraphs, as Wallace translates them, the words “thesis,” “antithesis,” and “synthesis” do not appear.

The understanding holds to the fixity of determinations and their distinction: it treats each as having a subsistence and a being of its own. On the dialectical side, these finite determinations sublate themselves and pass into their opposite. Hegel sees in this an inner tendency, by which the one-sidedness of the determinations of the understanding appears as their own negation, and he contrasts it with the habit of treating dialectic as an accidental art, which would introduce confusion into concepts. The speculative side, finally, grasps the unity of the terms in their opposition: the result of dialectic is positive, because it is not an empty nothing, but the negation of determinate propositions.

## Where the Triplet Comes From, Then

According to the Stanford Encyclopedia, Hegel was indeed influenced by Fichte, but he never adopted Fichte's triadic language of “thesis, antithesis, synthesis” to describe his own philosophy. He is said, on the other hand, to have used it in his lectures to describe Kant's philosophy (*Lectures on the History of Philosophy*, III, p. 477). The source says “apparently” and does not count the occurrences: one therefore cannot assert that he did so only once.

In Fichte, again according to the same encyclopedia, an “analytic or antithetic” reasoning brings out an opposition between the I and the not-I, then a “synthetic” reasoning resolves it by positing a third concept, that of divisibility.

Hegel moreover criticizes the formalist uses of “triplicity” inspired by Kant: they would be reduced to a lifeless schema, laid over contents like a mathematical formula. A scientific use of triplicity should, he says, flow from the inner life and the own movement of the content (*Phenomenology of Spirit*, §50 and 51, according to the SEP). The encyclopedia adds that this criticism may well be aimed at Fichte.

## What This Shifts

The SEP warns against applying the “textbook” example Being-Nothing-Becoming too dogmatically to the rest of the logic. The scheme may describe certain transitions, for example that from Measure to Essence, but, it writes, the development does not seem to conform to it in many more places. Even in that case, the measureless is first redefined as a measure (Encyclopedia, §109) before the transition to Essence.

Reading Hegel's dialectic as a sequence of three beats is therefore applying a formula from the outside, which Hegel himself reproached in the formalist uses of triplicity. In §81 of the Encyclopedia, the movement comes from within: it is the finite determinations themselves that sublate themselves and pass into their opposite.

repere.texte: Hegel never adopted, to describe his own philosophy, Fichte's triplet “thesis, antithesis, synthesis”; he is said to have used it, in his lectures, to describe Kant's philosophy (Lectures on the History of Philosophy, III, p. 477).

carte.punch: The “thesis, antithesis, synthesis” triangle associated with Hegel is Fichte's vocabulary.
carte.idee: Hegel describes his logic in three sides: abstract, dialectical, speculative. He did not adopt Fichte's triplet for his own philosophy, and he judges the formalist triplicity inspired by Kant a lifeless schema.

quiz.question: According to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, how does Hegel characterize the uses of triplicity inspired by Kant?
choix: As the very form of his own dialectic
As a lifeless schema, laid over contents
As a scientific method that must remain external to its content
As an invention of Hegel's, later taken up by Fichte
quiz.explication: The SEP reports that, for Hegel, these uses are reduced to “a lifeless schema,” imposed from the outside on contents, whereas a scientific use should flow from the content's own movement. It also specifies that he never adopted Fichte's triadic language for his own philosophy.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the text of the Encyclopedia (Wallace trans., §79 to 82), how many sides does Hegel distinguish in the logical doctrine?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hegel distinguishes three sides: the abstract (understanding), the dialectical (negative reason), and the speculative (positive reason), present in every concept.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the Stanford Encyclopedia, in what context would Hegel have used Fichte's triplet thesis, antithesis, synthesis?
choix: In the Encyclopedia, to describe his own logic
He never used it, not even for Kant
In his lectures, to describe Kant's philosophy
In the Phenomenology of Spirit, to describe his method
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The SEP indicates that he apparently used it in his lectures to sum up Kant's philosophy, Lectures on the History of Philosophy, III, p. 477, without applying it to his own philosophy.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In Fichte, according to the Stanford Encyclopedia, which concept does the synthetic reasoning that resolves the opposition between the I and the not-I arrive at?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Fichte's synthetic reasoning resolves the opposition between the I and the not-I by positing a third concept, that of divisibility, according to the SEP.
